unit.name: Live Theatre Review
unit.subtitle: How to analyse a production you have seen: performers, designers, directorial choices, and effect on the audience.

lessons.title: Watching Theatre Critically: Taking Useful Notes
lessons.description: How to watch a live production with an analytical eye and capture the detail you need for the written exam.
lessons.content_html:
Why Watching Is Not Enough

Most people leave a theatre humming the music or remembering the big emotional moments. For your live theatre review, that is not enough. The exam rewards you for being able to pinpoint specific choices — a performer's exact vocal quality at a named moment, the intensity and colour of a lighting state, the texture of a costume fabric — and then judge whether those choices successfully communicated meaning to the audience.

That level of detail requires a different kind of watching: critical spectatorship. This lesson gives you a framework for doing exactly that, both in the theatre and in the notes you write immediately afterwards.

Key Fact

The exam rewards specific technical detail, not general impressions. “The lighting was dark” earns no credit; “a single Fresnel special focused downstage centre, producing a cold blue wash at low intensity” can earn top marks.

The What / How / Why Framework

Before you enter the theatre, memorise this three-part scaffold. It structures every paragraph you will write in the exam:

  • What was the choice? Name it precisely: a sharp blackout, a sudden drop in the performer's vocal pitch, a costume change carried out in view of the audience.
  • How was it executed? Add technical detail: a Fresnel lantern at 20% intensity, a downward pitch shift of half an octave, a black linen coat replaced by a cream silk dress in full stage lighting.
  • Why did it work (or not)? Evaluate: what did the audience feel as a result? What meaning did the director intend to communicate? Did it succeed, and why?

This scaffold applies whether you are writing about a performer, a designer or the directorial concept. The key shift is from describing to evaluating.

Taking Notes in the Theatre

You cannot write full sentences in the dark, but you can capture trigger words that unlock memory later. Keep a small notepad and pencil. During the performance, note:

  • Performer moments: write the character's name, a one-word description of what the performer did, and a physical cue (e.g. “Mira — freeze — USL, turns away”). This helps you reconstruct the blocking later.
  • Design moments: note colour, direction and quality of the lighting state; any abrupt sound cues; unusual set elements. Even “blue wash — cold — interval end” is useful.
  • Audience reaction: if the audience gasped, laughed or fell silent at a particular moment, write it down. Audience response is evidence that a choice worked.
  • Stage configuration: sketch the stage layout in the margin — whether it is theatre in the round, a proscenium arch, or a thrust stage. This affects how proxemics read for the audience.

The interval is gold. Use the first five minutes to expand your shorthand notes while the first act is fresh. Ask yourself: what was the single most striking performer choice so far? What design element most affected my mood as an audience member? What do I think the director wants me to think about this production’s themes?

Write answers to these three questions in full sentences. You may use them almost verbatim in your exam. At the end of the second act, sit for two minutes before leaving — identify your most striking moment from the whole production before the crowd noise and adrenaline erase it.

Post-Show Notes: The Production Log

Write your production log within 24 hours of seeing the production. After that, specific sensory memories fade fast. Structure your log under four headings that match the exam’s focus:

  1. Production context: title, company, venue, date, stage configuration, approximate running time.
  2. Performer analysis: for each performer you plan to write about, record one vocal choice and one physical choice for a named moment, plus the effect on you as an audience member.
  3. Design analysis: one lighting example with technical details; one sound example; one set or costume observation. For each, note the specific moment and the audience effect.
  4. Directorial concept: in two or three sentences, state what you believe the director’s central intention was and give one piece of evidence for it.

Many students write a plot summary in their review — they retell what happened scene by scene. This earns little credit because the exam is asking you to analyse how meaning was communicated, not what the story was.

Think of the examiner as someone who also saw the production. They already know the plot. What they want to read is your analytical voice: why did a particular lighting state succeed in creating unease? Why did a performer’s sudden stillness communicate power more effectively than movement could have? That analytical perspective only comes from the What / How / Why scaffold, not from scene-by-scene summary.

Key Fact

The production you write about in the exam must be a live performance of at least 50 minutes, with at least two actors, dialogue and a range of production values. You may not write about your set play in the live theatre question.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
The most common mistake in the live theatre review is retelling the plot rather than evaluating specific choices. Examiners cannot give credit for “in the first scene the main character walks onto the stage and the lights fade.” They can give credit for: “at the opening, a single tungsten profile lit the performer from directly above, casting a sharp shadow downwards. The high contrast between the face in light and the body in shadow suggested the character’s isolation before a word had been spoken — the audience fell silent in response.”

Notice the difference: the second example names a lantern type, describes its direction and quality, names a moment, and evaluates the audience effect. Practise writing at this level of technical specificity in every note you take.

For any extended response, the What / How / Why scaffold is your insurance policy: it forces you to describe the choice, explain how it was executed with technical detail, and evaluate why it worked (or did not) for the audience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Critical spectatorship means watching with an analytical eye: identifying specific choices, noting technical details and observing audience reaction rather than simply following the story.
  • The What / How / Why scaffold structures every paragraph: name the choice, add technical detail, and evaluate the effect on the audience and the meaning communicated.
  • Write your production log within 24 hours, organised under four headings: production context, performer analysis, design analysis and directorial concept. Specific sensory detail fades quickly — record it before it does.

practice_questions.text: Give one thing you should note about a performer's vocal delivery when watching a live production.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: pitch / pace / pause / volume / accent / intonation / phrasing / emotional range / projection / timing. Accept any precise vocal skill.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'directorial concept'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it refers to the director's vision or intention; 1 mark for explaining that it shapes all performance and design decisions so the production communicates a unified meaning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how keeping a production log within 24 hours of seeing a performance helps a student write a stronger live theatre review.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying that specific detail fades quickly from memory; 1 mark for explaining that a log captures precise technical details (lantern type, colour, moment); 1 mark for explaining that these details support analytical writing rather than general impressions; 1 mark for linking this to the What / How / Why scaffold or to the exam's requirement for technical specificity.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the stage configuration of a production affects the way an audience experiences a performer's use of proxemics.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a named stage configuration (e.g. theatre in the round, proscenium arch, thrust stage); 1 mark for defining or explaining proxemics in the context of performer-audience relationship; 1 mark for analytical development of how the configuration changes how the audience reads spatial distance (e.g. in the round, every seat sees a different set of relationships; on a proscenium, the front-of-house sightline privileges downstage centre positions); 1 mark for a concrete example or evaluative statement about effect on audience.

practice_questions.text: Imagine you saw a production of a ghost story at a fictional touring theatre in 2024. In a key scene, the lead performer plays a character confronting the ghost for the first time. As a performer, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate the character's fear and disbelief at that moment. Refer to specific vocal and physical skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Response names at least one precise vocal choice (e.g. a sudden drop to near-whisper, broken phrasing with involuntary pauses, a rising pitch before the voice cracks) AND at least one precise physical choice (e.g. the body recoiling to upstage left, hands raised palms-outward, a sustained freeze of three beats before slow retreat), both anchored to this specific confrontation moment; effect on the audience is named and substantiated (e.g. the sudden stillness makes the audience hold its breath in empathy); language is technically fluent.
Secure (5-6): Names a vocal and a physical choice, generally anchored to the moment; explains at least one effect on the audience; mostly specific but may have one generic descriptor (e.g. 'her voice was quiet' without further detail).
Developing (3-4): Relevant choices mentioned but described in general terms ('she looked scared', 'her voice was soft'); little or no named effect on audience; limited technical vocabulary.
Emerging (1-2): Basic listing of general feelings or actions with no technical vocabulary and no reference to specific moment or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. In your answer, explain how specific performer choices and at least one design choice communicated meaning to the audience. Reach a substantiated evaluative judgement about how successfully meaning was communicated overall.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Sustained analytical writing anchored to named moments; every performer choice is specific (named vocal quality, named physical action, named moment); every design choice is concrete (lantern type, gobo, sound texture, costume fabric or colour); each choice is linked to a clearly stated effect on the audience; a confident, substantiated evaluative judgement is made about why the production succeeded or did not in communicating its central meaning; technical vocabulary used accurately throughout.
Secure (17-24): Most choices are specific; at least two performer choices and one design choice are named and explained with effect; an evaluative judgement is present though it may lack full substantiation; technical vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing (9-16): Relevant choices identified but often general ('the lighting was dark', 'the actor seemed sad'); some attempt at explaining effect on audience; little or no evaluative judgement; limited technical vocabulary.
Emerging (1-8): Largely descriptive or plot-based; choices listed rather than analysed; no evaluative judgement or audience effect; minimal technical vocabulary.

lessons.title: Analysing Performers: Vocal and Physical Choices
lessons.description: Pinpointing the specific acting choices that communicate character and meaning to an audience.
lessons.content_html:
From Feeling to Technique

When a performer moves an audience to tears, the temptation is to write “they were convincingly upset.” That sentence earns no marks. The exam rewards you for explaining how the performer created that effect: the precise vocal and physical skills they deployed and the meaning those skills communicated at that specific moment.

Vocal skills and physical skills are the two categories the spec identifies. Top-mark answers always name at least one from each category, anchor them to a specific moment in the production, and explain the effect on the audience.

Key Fact

Vocal skills include: pitch, pace, pause, volume, accent, intonation, phrasing, projection and timing. Physical skills include: posture, gesture, facial expression, movement, stillness, gait, spatial awareness and interaction with other performers.

Vocal Skills: The Language of Voice

Each vocal skill can be used to create a specific effect. Knowing which skill creates which effect is the key to strong analytical writing. Consider these:

  • Pitch: a sudden rise in pitch signals panic or excitement; a drop to the low register can convey threat, grief or resignation. The contrast between the two within a single speech is itself a technique — it shows the character’s instability.
  • Pace: rapid delivery can signal urgency or desperation; a deliberate, unhurried pace can communicate authority, menace or exhaustion. A performer who slows dramatically at the climax of a speech draws the audience in.
  • Pause: a well-placed silence is one of the most powerful tools a performer has. A three-second pause before a character’s answer can communicate internal conflict more precisely than any amount of text. Think of it as a word the playwright left blank for the performer to fill.
  • Volume: a performer who drops from normal conversational volume to near-inaudible draws the audience physically forward in their seats; a sudden shout after sustained quiet is a physical shock. Both are intentional choices.
  • Intonation and phrasing: the rising or falling melody of a sentence, and where the performer chooses to breathe and break their line, controls where the audience focuses its attention.

Physical Skills: The Language of the Body

Tableau and stillness are often more powerful than movement. When a performer freezes in the middle of chaotic action, every audience member looks at them immediately. That is focus achieved through physical discipline, not scenery.

Other physical skills to analyse include:

  • Posture: an upright, expansive posture reads as power or confidence across the room; a collapsed, inward posture reads as vulnerability or defeat. If the posture shifts within a scene, the character’s status has shifted — note exactly when it changes.
  • Gesture: gestures can be open (arms extended, palms up — invitation) or closed (arms crossed, hands pulled in — self-protection). A single raised hand can silence a stage; a pointing finger can be an accusation. Analyse the gesture, not just its name.
  • Facial expression: the micro-expressions that pass across a performer’s face in a close-focus moment are often what an audience remembers most vividly. If the performer’s expression contradicted the character’s words — a smile that didn’t reach the eyes, a flash of doubt suppressed — that subtext is gold for analysis.
  • Movement and gait: how a character crosses the stage communicates as much as what they say. A heavy, deliberate walk implies weight (emotional or literal); a light, darting movement implies anxiety or calculation.

Imagine you saw a fictional touring production of a kitchen-sink drama in 2024. In the climactic argument scene, the lead performer playing the mother confronted the adult son. Here is how you might write about that moment:

Weak version (no marks at this level): “The actress playing the mother was very emotional and you could tell she was upset. She looked like she was going to cry.”

Strong version: “In the moment when the mother finally confronted her son, the performer dropped her vocal pace to almost half its previous rate and allowed a three-beat pause after each sentence, as though each word cost her something. Simultaneously, her physical posture collapsed inward — shoulders drawn forward, spine curved, eyes cast downward rather than meeting his — so that despite her status as parent, she visually occupied less stage space than her adult son. This juxtaposition — a parent whose voice is measured and powerful but whose body has surrendered — communicated the complexity of her grief: she was both holding herself together and falling apart simultaneously. The audience became very still at this moment, which suggested the choice was communicating its intended meaning effectively.”

Notice: one vocal skill (pace and pause), one physical skill (posture and use of stage space), a specific moment, a named effect on the audience, and an evaluative judgement. That is the formula for a top-band paragraph.

Interaction and Ensemble

In your review, do not only write about individual performers in isolation. Ensemble moments — where the company moves, speaks or responds as a single unit — are often the most theatrically powerful. When an ensemble suddenly splits apart, or when all performers simultaneously turn to face the audience, the effect is difficult to achieve and, when it works, is deeply affecting.

Analyse the interaction between two performers as you would a single performer: what did the proxemics between them tell you? Did one performer physically diminish themselves to elevate the other? Did a brief moment of eye contact or its conspicuous absence change the mood of the scene?

A persistent error is to describe the character’s inner state rather than the performer’s external technique. Phrases like “she was angry,” “he seemed afraid” and “you could feel her sadness” describe emotions, not skills. They tell the examiner nothing about how the performer communicated the emotion.

The fix is simple: ask yourself, “what did the performer actually do with their voice or body?” Then describe that. “She was angry” becomes “her volume escalated across the scene until by the final line she was projecting at full strength from upstage right, her jaw tense and her hands forming fists at her sides.” That is performer technique, not emotional description.

Key Fact

Every time you write about a performer, you need both a vocal AND a physical choice. One alone is not enough for an 8-mark or 32-mark answer. Train yourself to pair them: “vocally she… / physically she…”
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For questions asking you to interpret or analyse a performer, the most common error is to write about what the character is feeling without translating that into specific vocal and physical choices. “I would act scared” is not a technique; “I would lower my volume to a near-whisper, increase the pace of my delivery and physically back away to upstage right while maintaining eye contact with the antagonist” is.

Always pair vocal and physical: the examiner looks for both. If you only address one category, you cannot reach the top band regardless of how detailed you are. A useful self-check: count your vocal skills and your physical skills in your draft answer. If either column is empty, add to it before you move on.

In the 32-mark live theatre review, anchor every performer observation to a named moment (not “throughout the play”). The more specific the moment, the more analytical your writing can be.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Performer analysis requires both vocal skills (pitch, pace, pause, volume, intonation, phrasing) and physical skills (posture, gesture, facial expression, movement, stillness) — always name one of each and anchor them to a specific moment.
  • Describe what the performer did, not how the character felt: “she lowered her pitch and allowed a three-beat pause” is analytical; “she seemed sad” is not.
  • Ensemble interaction and proxemics between performers are equally valid subjects for analysis — the spatial relationship between two characters at a key moment can communicate meaning as powerfully as any single performer choice.

practice_questions.text: Identify one vocal skill a performer might use to communicate a character's authority.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: a slow, measured pace / a low pitch / a loud, projected volume / a deliberate pause before speaking / a clipped, precise intonation. Accept any precise vocal skill linked plausibly to authority.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'tableau'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it is a still, frozen stage picture; 1 mark for explaining that it uses the positions and relationships of performers' bodies to communicate meaning without movement or speech.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer's use of stillness at a key moment in a live production can have a powerful effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what stillness is (a deliberate absence of movement at a chosen moment); 1 mark for explaining how it draws focus (the eye is drawn to the still performer amid movement, or to the performer whose stillness signals internal change); 1 mark for a specific audience effect (e.g. the audience becomes quiet, leans in, anticipates what comes next); 1 mark for a developed link to meaning or character (e.g. stillness can communicate suppressed emotion, moral weight or a moment of decision more powerfully than action).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the interaction between two performers in the live production you have seen communicated the relationship between their characters at a specific moment.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for naming a specific moment or scene; 1 mark for identifying a specific interaction (e.g. one performer's gaze held, broken or avoided; the proxemic distance decreasing or increasing; a gesture directed at rather than away from the other); 1 mark for analytical development of what the interaction communicated about the characters' relationship (power, intimacy, conflict, dependency); 1 mark for a statement about audience effect or evaluative comment on how effectively the relationship was communicated.

practice_questions.text: Imagine you saw a fictional community theatre production of a tragedy in 2025. In the final scene, the lead performer playing the protagonist discovers they have caused the death of someone they loved. As a performer in that role, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate the character's shock and guilt to the audience. Refer to specific vocal and physical skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Names at least one precise vocal choice (e.g. voice drops to near-silence; all pace is stripped away so delivery becomes word by single word; a sharp intake of breath before speech begins) AND at least one precise physical choice (e.g. the body sinks from standing to crouching over the figure on the floor; hands reach out but stop short of touching; the face tilts up toward the audience then immediately turns away), both anchored clearly to this discovery moment; the effect on the audience is named and substantiated (e.g. the silence in the auditorium confirmed the audience was holding this moment with the performer); language is technically fluent throughout.
Secure (5-6): Names a vocal and a physical choice, generally anchored to the moment; audience effect explained for at least one choice; mostly specific but may contain one general descriptor.
Developing (3-4): Relevant choices present but described in general or emotional terms; little technical vocabulary; limited link to audience effect.
Emerging (1-2): Basic emotional description with no technical vocabulary and no specific moment or audience effect identified.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. Focus specifically on the vocal and physical choices made by one performer in a key moment. Explain how those choices communicated meaning and evaluate how successfully they worked for the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Sustained analytical writing focused on a clearly named moment; at least two vocal choices and at least two physical choices are named with technical precision (not just 'louder' but 'projected from the diaphragm with the volume rising across the final three lines'); each choice is linked to a specific, named audience effect; an evaluative judgement is reached that is substantiated by the evidence given; terminology used accurately and fluently throughout.
Secure (17-24): At least one vocal and one physical choice named and explained with effect; some technical vocabulary; evaluative judgement present though may not be fully substantiated; generally anchored to a specific moment.
Developing (9-16): Choices identified but described in general emotional terms; some relevant vocabulary; some attempt at audience effect; limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-8): Largely descriptive or plot-based; minimal technical vocabulary; no evaluative judgement.

glossary_terms.definition: The measurable technical skills a performer uses with their voice to communicate character, emotion and meaning, including pitch, pace, pause, volume, intonation, phrasing and accent.

The unstated meaning beneath a character's words, communicated by the performer through vocal and physical choices rather than the script itself.

lessons.title: Analysing Design: Set, Lighting, Sound, Costume
lessons.description: Reading design choices in a production and explaining the meanings they generate for the audience.
lessons.content_html:
Design Is Not Decoration

A common misconception is that set, lighting, sound and costume are the “backdrop” to the real action of the performers. In any well-made production, design is as much a language as speech. A single lighting choice — a green wash sliding in at the moment a character tells their first lie — can communicate to the audience something the dialogue never says. Your job in the exam is to decode that language.

The principle is the same as for performers: name the specific design choice, explain how it was executed technically, and evaluate its effect on the audience. The vocabulary is different — you are now working in lantern types, gobos, underscore, set materials — but the analytical method is identical.

Key Fact

Design vocabulary the examiner rewards: Fresnel (soft-edged wash), profile (hard-edged beam), flood (wide area wash), moving light, gobo (patterned effect), gel (colour filter), lighting special (a single focused lantern on one area), blackout, cross-fade, lighting state.

Lighting: Four Questions to Ask

When you observe a lighting moment in a production, run through four questions:

  1. Direction: where is the light coming from? Front lighting is naturalistic; side lighting gives a dramatic split-face effect and implies conflict or duality; top lighting isolates and can suggest divine or oppressive power; back lighting creates silhouette, suggesting mystery or the loss of individual identity.
  2. Colour: what gel or filter is being used? Cool blues and greens signal isolation, threat or the supernatural; warm ambers and yellows signal domestic warmth, nostalgia or golden-age memory; deep red can signal passion, danger or violence. The specific combination matters — a blue wash with a single warm special on one character separates them from the world around them.
  3. Intensity: what is the brightness? A fade to near-darkness before a final moment creates dread; a sudden full-white wash can feel clinical, exposing, accusatory. The rate of the fade or the snap of the change is also a choice — a snap blackout shocks; a slow two-minute fade mourns.
  4. Equipment and effect: if a gobo projects bars across the stage, does that suggest imprisonment? If a lighting special follows a character across the stage, does that suggest they are watched, celebrated or exposed? Note the effect, not just the equipment.

Imagine you saw a fictional production of a thriller at a hypothetical studio theatre in 2025. In the penultimate scene, the villain revealed their true identity to the protagonist. Consider how a strong analysis might read:

Weak version: “The lighting was dark and dramatic, which suited the tense mood.”

Strong version: “As the villain turned to face the protagonist, the stage lighting cross-faded from a warm amber general wash to a single cold tungsten profile focused tightly on the villain’s face from a steeply raked angle above and stage left. The cross-fade took approximately four seconds, so by the time the speech began the protagonist’s face had vanished into shadow while the villain’s was fully lit — a visual metaphor for the shift in power within the scene. The bar gobo projected across the downstage area suggested confinement; the protagonist was already, in lighting terms, trapped before a word had been spoken. The effect on the audience was palpable: the laughter from earlier scenes disappeared completely, replaced by a sustained, uncomfortable silence.”

Notice: lantern type (profile), direction (steeply raked, stage left), colour (cold tungsten), a gobo type (bar), the rate of the change (four seconds), the metaphorical meaning and a specific audience reaction. All from one lighting cue.

Sound: Diegetic, Non-Diegetic and Soundscape

Diegetic sound is sound the characters can hear; non-diegetic sound is heard only by the audience. A creaking door is diegetic; the unsettling low-frequency drone beneath a scene of domestic abuse is non-diegetic underscore. Both can be analysed for meaning.

When analysing sound, note: the texture of the sound (is it crisp and close, or distant and reverberant?), its placement (coming from specific speakers — stage left, from above, or surrounding the audience?), its relationship to the action (does it start before the scene begins, establishing mood before the performers enter?), and any sudden change (a silence that was filled with underscore is often more powerful than the music itself).

A soundscape is a layered sonic environment rather than a single cue: the simultaneous combination of rain, distant thunder, traffic and an indistinct crowd for an opening city scene, for instance. Note how many layers you can identify and what the cumulative effect was.

Set and Costume: Symbol and Material

Set designers make choices about material, colour, scale, level and symbolic meaning. A single chair on an otherwise bare stage can communicate isolation, power or waiting. A set that rotates during the performance communicates flux, the relentlessness of time, or the character’s inability to escape their world. When analysing set, note: what objects are present and what they symbolise; whether the set changed during the performance and what the change communicated; the relationship between the set’s scale and the performer’s body (a small figure dwarfed by an enormous set reads as the individual overwhelmed by forces beyond their control).

For costume, examiners want specific fabric, colour and silhouette analysis, not just era or genre. A costume that is visually impeccable but slightly too large for the performer communicates something very different from one that fits perfectly. Note colour against the set and against other characters’ costumes — if every character wears grey and one wears deep scarlet, that contrast is a design intention, not an accident.

Students frequently write design analysis at a level of generality that earns little credit: “the lighting was atmospheric,” “the costumes were period-appropriate,” “there was dramatic music.” These sentences do not tell the examiner anything analytical.

Compare “the costumes were period-appropriate” with “the lead character’s costume was a knee-length coat in heavyweight charcoal wool with a silhouette that was structured at the shoulders and narrowed at the waist, giving the performer the physical presence of authority even when standing still.” Both sentences are about costume. Only one demonstrates that you understand how design communicates meaning.

The rule is simple: if you cannot say which lantern, what colour, which fabric and what effect, your note-taking in the theatre was not specific enough. Build the habit of technical precision at the performance itself.

Key Fact

Design disciplines to cover in your review: lighting (lantern type, direction, colour, intensity, gobo, lighting state), sound (diegetic / non-diegetic, texture, placement, underscore, soundscape), set (material, level, scale, symbolic props), costume (colour, fabric, silhouette, fit).
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For questions asking you to analyse design choices, the most common error is describing general mood rather than naming specific elements. “The lighting was dark and scary” earns no credit. “A Fresnel flood at 15% intensity with a deep blue gel created a cold, low-contrast environment in which every performer appeared shadowless and exposed” earns marks at every level.

For the 8-mark designer question, you must specify a design discipline (lighting, sound, set or costume) and name concrete elements within it — lantern type, gobo, fabric, colour, fitting. Justify each choice with reference to the moment’s meaning or the directorial intention. Generic descriptors like “dark mood” or “period costume” alone do not demonstrate design knowledge.

In the 32-mark live theatre review, you must address at least one design discipline alongside your performer analysis. The mark scheme rewards responses that show the interaction between performance and design — how a performer’s vocal choice and a lighting state worked together at a specific moment to produce a combined effect on the audience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Design analysis requires specific technical vocabulary: lantern type, direction, colour, intensity and gobo for lighting; diegetic or non-diegetic, texture, placement and soundscape for sound; fabric, colour, silhouette and fit for costume; material, scale, level and symbolic meaning for set.
  • Run four questions on any lighting moment you observe: What is the direction? What is the colour? What is the intensity? What equipment or effect is being used and what does it mean?
  • General descriptions earn no marks. If you cannot specify which lantern, which colour and which effect at a named moment, return to your production notes and find more detail before you write.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of lantern used in stage lighting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: Fresnel / profile / flood / moving light / birdie / strobe. Accept any legitimate lantern type from theatrical practice.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'soundscape'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape is made up of multiple sound layers; 1 mark for explaining that the layers are combined to create an immersive sonic environment that establishes location, period or mood for the audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer's use of a gobo can communicate meaning to the audience at a specific moment in a production.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately defining a gobo as a shaped template inside a lantern that projects a pattern of light; 1 mark for naming or describing a specific pattern (e.g. bar gobo suggesting imprisonment, leaf gobo suggesting a natural environment, window-frame gobo placing the action inside a building); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the audience's reading of the scene (e.g. the bars reinforce the theme of confinement visually even as the dialogue speaks of freedom); 1 mark for a developed evaluative statement or link to directorial intention.

practice_questions.text: In the live production you have seen, explain how one lighting choice and one sound choice worked together at a specific moment to create meaning for the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Identifies a specific moment in the production; names a precise lighting choice (lantern type, colour, direction, intensity or effect) and a precise sound choice (type, texture, placement, diegetic or non-diegetic status); analyses how the two choices worked in combination to create a specific audience effect; makes an analytical statement about what the director was trying to communicate through this design combination; language is technically fluent and uses accurate terminology throughout.
Secure (7-9): Both a lighting and a sound choice are named and explained with reasonable specificity; audience effect is identified; some analysis of intention present; mostly accurate terminology.
Developing (4-6): Lighting and sound choices identified but described generally; limited technical vocabulary; some attempt at effect or intention but not developed.
Emerging (1-3): General descriptions only; no technical vocabulary; no analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Imagine you are a lighting designer working on a fictional production of a ghost story at a hypothetical studio theatre. In the scene where the protagonist first sees the ghost, design the lighting state you would use. Refer to specific lighting choices and explain their intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Names at least two specific lighting elements (e.g. a cold profile special at steep angle from above stage right for the ghost; a Fresnel wash in a deep blue-green gel across the full stage; a bar gobo projected across the protagonist suggesting entrapment); each choice is justified with reference to its intended audience effect (e.g. the steep top-light creates deep shadows on the ghost's face that deny the audience a clear identity for the figure, creating unease); language is technically fluent.
Secure (5-6): At least two lighting choices named and justified; audience effect explained for at least one; generally specific but may have one general descriptor.
Developing (3-4): Relevant lighting ideas present but described in general terms (e.g. 'I would make the lighting dark and spooky'); limited technical vocabulary; effect mentioned but not developed.
Emerging (1-2): One or two general lighting ideas with no technical vocabulary and no link to audience effect or design intention.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. In your answer, focus on how the design choices (in at least two design disciplines) communicated meaning to the audience. Reach a substantiated evaluative judgement about how successfully the design realised the directorial concept.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Detailed, sustained analysis of at least two design disciplines; every design choice is named with technical specificity (lantern type, gobo, gel colour, fabric, soundscape texture); every choice is anchored to a named moment and linked to a stated audience effect; the response evaluates the overall success of the design in realising the directorial concept with substantiated judgement; fluent technical language throughout.
Secure (17-24): At least two design disciplines addressed with reasonable specificity; audience effect identified for most choices; an evaluative judgement present; some technical language.
Developing (9-16): Design choices identified but described generally; limited technical vocabulary; some attempt at audience effect; limited or absent evaluative judgement.
Emerging (1-8): Largely descriptive; one discipline only or very general across both; no technical vocabulary; no evaluative judgement.

glossary_terms.definition: A shaped template placed inside a lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage, such as window bars, leaves or abstract shapes.
A specific combination of lanterns active at a given moment, defined by direction, colour, intensity and type.
A single lantern focused on one small area of the stage, creating an isolated pool of light around one performer or object.

Sound that exists outside the world of the play and is heard only by the audience, such as a musical underscore.

A broad, even spread of light from a flood or Fresnel lantern covering a large area of the stage to establish general atmosphere.

lessons.title: Effect on the Audience: Evaluation Beyond Description
lessons.description: Moving from describing what you saw to judging how successfully meaning was communicated and why.
lessons.content_html:
The Gap Between Description and Evaluation

There is a significant and frequently tested gap between describing a production and evaluating it. Description tells the examiner what you saw: “the performer crossed to downstage centre and the lighting faded to a single warm special.” Evaluation tells the examiner what it meant and whether it worked: “by isolating the performer downstage centre in a warm special while the ensemble faded to shadow upstage, the director communicated the character’s separation from their community at the moment of crisis — an effect that was reinforced by the audience’s collective silence.”

The 32-mark live theatre review specifically rewards substantiated evaluative judgement. That means you cannot simply state that a choice was “effective” — you must say why it was effective, with what evidence, and sometimes weigh it against moments where it was less successful.

Key Fact

A substantiated evaluative judgement has three parts: (1) a clear statement of the judgement (the choice succeeded / partially succeeded / did not achieve its intention), (2) a specific reason (the technical detail that made it work or fail), and (3) evidence (audience response, the coherence of the choice with the directorial concept, or a comparison with another moment).

What Is a Directorial Concept?

Every well-made production has a directorial concept: a central idea or question that the production is trying to explore, and which shapes every performer and design choice. When you evaluate a production, you are asking not just “did this choice work?” but “did this choice serve the directorial concept?”

For example, imagine a fictional production of a Victorian social drama at a hypothetical regional theatre in 2024 where the director set the play in a modern corporate office. In that context, every performer and design choice has a conceptual function: the sharp-edged glass and chrome set communicates the coldness of institutional power; the identical blue-grey suits worn by all characters except the protagonist suggest conformity; the sudden moment when the protagonist arrives in warm terracotta communicates her separateness before she says a word. Each of these choices succeeds if it reinforces the concept and fails if it contradicts it without purpose.

Audience Response as Evidence

One of the most powerful pieces of evidence you can use in your evaluation is the audience’s response. You were in the auditorium; you experienced the production’s effect collectively. If the audience gasped, laughed unexpectedly, fell completely silent or shifted restlessly, those are observable, real responses to specific theatrical choices.

Use this evidence explicitly: “the audience fell entirely silent for the four seconds of the blackout before the final scene, which confirmed that the director’s choice had successfully built anticipation over the preceding hour.” That sentence is evaluative, specific and evidenced. Compare it with: “the blackout was effective at the end.” The same word — “effective” — appears in both, but only the first sentence earns marks.

Imagine a fictional touring production of a Greek myth-inspired play at a hypothetical arts centre in 2024. In the final scene, the protagonist accepted their fate and knelt centre stage as the ensemble moved silently in a circle around them.

Description (no evaluation): “The protagonist knelt in the middle of the stage and the other actors walked in a circle around them. The lights went dark except for one bright light above the protagonist. The music was quiet and sad.”

Evaluation: “The director’s decision to place the protagonist kneeling at centre stage while the ensemble moved in a slow clockwise circle communicated the character’s willing surrender to forces beyond their control. The use of a high-intensity tungsten profile lantern focused from directly above — a top-light that created a perfect circle of light around the static figure — reinforced the symbolism: the character had become both the centre of the world and its prisoner simultaneously. The underscore, a sustained cello line at low volume that had been building for the previous three minutes, reached its resolution and then stopped completely as the protagonist bowed their head. The resulting silence lasted approximately six seconds before the snap blackout. The audience did not move or speak for several seconds after the lights returned, which suggests the production had succeeded in communicating the weight of the moment.”

Both paragraphs describe the same moment. Only the second one evaluates it — and only the second one earns marks in the top band.

The Language of Evaluation

Examiners are trained to look for evaluative language. Certain phrases signal that you are evaluating rather than describing. Build these into your vocabulary:

  • This succeeded in communicating… because… (names the success, names the reason)
  • This choice was particularly effective at this moment because… (links the choice to the specific moment)
  • The effect on the audience was… which suggests the director intended… (links audience response to directorial intention)
  • While this worked in the earlier scene, here it was less convincing because… (balanced evaluation, showing critical perspective)
  • The most memorable moment was… because… and this supported the overall concept of the production by… (integrates a judgement with the directorial concept)

Notice that every evaluative phrase contains “because” or “which suggests” or “by.” Evaluation always requires reasoning. A judgement without a reason is just an opinion.

Themes and Subtext

Subtext operates at every level of a production. A director who cuts a scene short, or who allows one character to remain on stage in silence after others have exited, is creating subtext through structure and staging. When you evaluate, you can acknowledge subtext as a layer of meaning: “the performer’s choice to hold the gaze of the audience for three seconds after the final line — before the blackout cut off the eye contact — communicated that the character was aware of being observed, and perhaps complicit in their own fate.”

Strong evaluative writing connects the moment to the theme: not just “this made the audience feel sad” but “this communicated the production’s central theme of inevitable loss, and the audience’s collective silence was evidence that the communication had succeeded.”

Many students believe that evaluation simply means saying “I thought it was brilliant” or “I think the director did a great job.” Unsubstantiated opinion earns the lowest marks in the top-band mark scheme.

The difference is substance: an evaluative judgement is a claim supported by specific theatrical evidence. “I thought the set was very impressive” is opinion without evidence. “The set’s decision to use a raked platform rising from stage right to upstage left forced every performer to hold themselves slightly off-balance when standing still, which communicated the physical precariousness of the characters’ social positions and was consistently effective throughout the production” is a substantiated evaluative judgement. Train yourself to follow every judgement with “because” and a specific theatrical detail.

Key Fact

Evaluation always requires: a judgement + a reason + evidence. If any of the three parts is missing, it is either description (no judgement), assertion (no reason) or generalisation (no evidence). All three parts must appear in top-band answers.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
In the 32-mark live theatre review, the examiner looks specifically for a “substantiated evaluative judgement.” This means your conclusion or summative statement must do three things: state clearly whether the production succeeded in communicating its central meaning, give at least one specific reason drawn from a named moment, and acknowledge any areas where the communication was less successful or where you had a reservations about a choice.

The most frequent reason students fall out of the top band is that they describe beautifully but never move into evaluation. Check your answer: have you used “because,” “which suggests,” “this succeeded in communicating” or “this was less effective because”? If none of those phrases appear, you have described but not evaluated.

For the 12-mark analyse intentions question, the analytical method is the same as evaluation but focused specifically on what the playwright or director intended the audience to think, feel or understand at a particular moment. Always name the intention, name the theatrical method used to achieve it, and judge whether the method succeeded.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Evaluation is not opinion: it is a judgement supported by specific theatrical evidence. Every evaluative claim must be followed by “because” and a technical reason drawn from a named moment in the production.
  • Audience response is valid evidence: if the audience laughed, gasped or fell silent at a specific moment, that response is proof that a choice communicated its intended meaning — use it explicitly in your review.
  • A substantiated evaluative judgement has three parts: a clear verdict (succeeded / partially succeeded / did not succeed), a specific reason (the technical detail that made it work or fail), and evidence (audience response, coherence with directorial concept, or comparison with another moment).

practice_questions.text: Give one word that describes language used to make a judgement about the effectiveness of a theatrical choice.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: evaluative / analytical / critical / judgement-based. Accept any precise term that accurately names language expressing a reasoned assessment of effectiveness.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'subtext' in the context of live theatre analysis?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that subtext is unstated meaning beneath the surface action; 1 mark for explaining that it is communicated through theatrical choices (performer, staging or design) rather than through explicit dialogue.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use the positioning of a performer on stage after other performers have exited to communicate subtext to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying that the lingering performer attracts focus because they are the only figure on stage; 1 mark for explaining the staging choice (e.g. the performer remains centre stage, or moves to a specific position that carries symbolic weight in the production); 1 mark for the audience effect (e.g. the audience reads isolation, guilt, unresolved conflict or the weight of a decision on the character); 1 mark for a link to subtext, directorial concept or a broader theme of the production.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how one specific moment in the live production you have seen communicated a theme of the production to the audience. Refer to both a performer choice and a design choice in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a named moment and a theme; 1 mark for naming a specific performer choice at that moment and briefly explaining how it communicated the theme; 1 mark for naming a specific design choice at that moment and briefly explaining how it communicated the theme; 1 mark for an analytical statement about how the two choices worked together or for an evaluative comment on the effectiveness of the communication.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the director of the live production you have seen communicated the production's central theme to the audience. Refer to specific theatrical choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Identifies a clear directorial concept or central theme; names at least two specific theatrical choices (from performance and/or design) that communicate this theme; analyses how each choice serves the directorial intention rather than just describing it; evaluates how successfully the theme was communicated overall with a substantiated judgement; technically fluent language throughout.
Secure (7-9): Directorial concept identified; at least two choices named and linked to theme; some evaluative language; generally specific but may be uneven in technical detail.
Developing (4-6): Relevant choices identified but analysis stays at surface level; theme identified but choices not clearly linked to it; limited technical vocabulary.
Emerging (1-3): Description of plot or general impressions; no identifiable directorial concept; no analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. In your answer, explain how the director communicated meaning through specific performer and design choices. Reach a substantiated evaluative judgement about how successfully the production communicated its central themes to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Sustained analytical writing that moves consistently between description of specific choices and evaluation of their effect; at least two performer choices (one vocal, one physical) and at least two design choices (across at least two disciplines) are named with technical precision; each choice is anchored to a named moment; directorial concept is identified and choices are evaluated against it; a clear, substantiated evaluative judgement about overall success is reached, supported by specific evidence including audience response; technically fluent throughout.
Secure (17-24): Performer and design choices present and mostly specific; audience effect identified; some evaluation of directorial concept; a judgement reached though not always fully substantiated; technical vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing (9-16): Relevant choices identified; some attempt at linking to audience effect or theme; evaluation attempted but often unsubstantiated opinion; limited technical vocabulary.
Emerging (1-8): Largely plot summary or description; no evaluative judgement; minimal technical vocabulary; choices listed without analysis.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following sentences contains a substantiated evaluative judgement?
options: The lighting was very effective and impressive.
The performer walked to the centre of the stage.
The top-light isolated the performer, communicating their separation from the ensemble, which was confirmed by the audience's collective silence.
I thought the set design was brilliant.

knowledge_checks.q: What is a directorial concept?

The script and stage directions written by the playwright
The process of auditioning performers for a production
The lighting plot designed for a specific production

knowledge_checks.q: A substantiated evaluative judgement requires three parts: a verdict, a _____, and evidence.

Match each type of statement to its category:
left: 'The blackout was effective because it cut off the audience's final view of the character, leaving their fate unresolved.'
right: General impression (no marks at high level)

glossary_terms.definition: A reasoned judgement about the effectiveness of a theatrical choice, supported by evidence from specific moments in the production.
The overarching artistic vision shaping all performance and design decisions so the production communicates a unified set of meanings to the audience.
The unstated meanings beneath the surface action of a play, communicated through theatrical choices rather than explicit dialogue.
A complete absence of light on stage, usually achieved abruptly to punctuate a scene or create shock.
The collective reaction of the audience at a specific moment, such as silence, laughter or a gasp, used as evidence that a theatrical choice communicated its intended meaning.
A reasoned judgement about how successfully a theatrical choice communicated meaning, supported by specific technical evidence and an analysis of audience effect.
Writing that examines how theatrical choices create meaning, rather than simply describing what happened in a production.
The process by which a production's design and performance choices work together to convey its central ideas or themes to the audience.
